newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH SOCIALIST LEADER PREPARES TO GOVERN.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH SOCIALIST LEADER PREPARES TO GOVERN.

text.p: The leader of France's left, sounding increasingly confident of victory in Sunday's parliamentary election, urged conservative President Jacques Chirac on Thursday to prepare to let him govern.

"On Sunday, if it is resolved in favour of a government of change, the president will certainly have to let us govern, just as we will have to respect his prerogatives," said Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin, who would head the government should the left prevail in the National Assembly poll.

But France's Communist Party, perhaps feeling queasy about joining forces with a group that did not share many of its goals, threatened not to join a leftist government though it pledged its loyalty in any case.

Alain Bocquet, president of the Communist group in the outgoing National Assembly, told a rally in the northern city of Lille the Communists would be loyal "whether we participate in a government or whether we support it without participating".
That raised the prospect of the Communists seeking no ministers in a leftist cabinet. Bocquet said a decision would be made at a mass party meeting on Monday.
The Communists had taken a similar stance towards a leftist government in 1984, withdrawing its ministers from the cabinet and denouncing a Socialist "turn to the right".

Some analysts speculate that the left, which won an upset victory over the current centre-right majority in last Sunday's first-round vote, might win enough seats in the Sunday runoff to have a National Assembly majority without help from Communists.
But Bocquet's statement could also mean that hardliners within his party had argued against joining a Socialist-led government so as not to compromise their ideals.

Even outgoing rightist Prime Minister Alain Juppe conceded the Socialist-led opposition could win the decisive runoff and pleaded with his backers in a radio interview to campaign "with a bit more fire and passion" in the dying days of the race.

Juppe stepped down this week, taking the blame for the right's first-round defeat following Chirac's call for an early election, in hopes of giving France a "new elan" and a renewed majority for the shift to a single European currency.

Even some senior centrists in the ruling coalition voiced dismay at a tandem of socially-minded National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin and free-marketeer Alain Madelin, thrust into the limelight in a last-ditch attempt to regain momentum.
"This is an impossible couple of the least social and the most anti-European," Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin said of the pair.
Seguin, who has called on the government to take a bigger role in battling record 12.8 percent unemployment, has been tipped as prime minister in case of a rightist victory.
Former finance minister Madelin, who wants big cuts in the state's role, has been tipped as finance minister.
Seguin, addressing a rally in Paris, said rightist voters had rejected the majority coalition last Sunday because they had not been given a clear picture of its plans.

"They want a road map which explains to them what we expect of them, where we want to lead them," he said. "If we do not do so now, their anger will continue to grow and will end up engulfing us all, both the majority and the opposition."

"We must mobilise all of our energies, here and now, against unemployment," Seguin said. "No one, to my knowledge, has invented a vaccine against unemployment. But we can attack it from many directions, by focusing our resources."
Stocks in the Paris bourse's CAC index closed 0.15 percent lower on Thursday, still jittery after the index plunged 3.6 percent on Wednesday on speculation about a left-wing win. REUTER
